place.en: The Silver-leaf Vale · the foot of the cliff

setup.zh: 崖根下两块大石头中间，躺着一个比你还小的孩子，腰折了，一只手攥着白布口袋，一只手捏着半张烧焦的黄纸。
setup.en: Between two boulders at the foot of the cliff lies a child smaller than you, his back broken; one hand clutches a white cloth sack, the other half a sheet of scorched yellow paper.

recap.zh: 谷底崖根下，一个叫锁儿的孩子死在你手里。他是穿白的老爷拿一锭银子雇进岭来逮白狐狸的；那锭圈里一横的银子，如今在你怀里。
recap.en: At the foot of the cliff a child called Suo'er died holding your hand. A gentleman in white had hired him with a silver ingot to catch a white fox in the ridge; that ingot, stamped with a circle and a stroke, is in your jacket now.

en: At the foot of the cliff, a child.
"He called me back… I couldn't find the way."
A silver ingot: a circle, and a stroke across it.

story.zh:
他爬过去。左手腕一撑地，疼得眼前一黑，他便拿右手和两个膝盖爬。崖根下两块大石头中间，躺着一个孩子。

那孩子比他还小，看着不过十岁，瘦得一把骨头，一件单褂湿透了贴在身上，补丁比小满的还多。他仰面躺着，腰底下硌着一块棱角朝上的石头，身子从腰那里折成一个古怪的样子，两条腿摊在泥水里，一动也不动。

他一只手死死攥着一只白布口袋，另一只手里，捏着半张黄纸，黄纸的一头烧焦了。

他听见有人来，眼珠子转过来，看见了小满，嘴唇动了动：「……是来接我的么？」

小满道：「我是石坳村的。我也掉下来了。」

那孩子眼睛里那一点亮，便暗下去了。

小满伸手要去扶他，手刚碰着他的肩膀，那孩子「啊」的一声，声音不大，却叫得小满的手像给火燎了，再不敢碰。他爹说过，山里摔断了腰的野物，不能挪，挪一回，死一回。他便跪在泥水里，把身子往前探，挡在那孩子脸上头，替他挡雨。

「你叫什么？」

「锁儿。」那孩子道，「长命锁的锁。我娘给起的。」他喘了两口，「锁早当了。」

「哪个村的？」

锁儿没答这一句。他道：「……哥，有吃的没有？」

小满把怀里的东西都掏了出来。他娘那张饼裹在布里，湿了一角；阿禾那个鸡蛋，还囫囵着。他把鸡蛋在石头上磕了，一点一点剥干净，剥出白生生的一个，递到锁儿嘴边。

锁儿张了张嘴，咬不动，只拿鼻子凑上去闻了闻，闻了很久，道：「香。」便不吃了。小满攥着那个鸡蛋，不知道往哪里放。

锁儿忽然说起话来，一句接一句，说得很急，生怕说慢了，后头便没工夫说了。

「有个穿白的老爷……到我们那儿……挑孩子。挑瘦的，挑没爹的。他说那碑不让他进，只让小孩进。他说岭里有一只白狐狸，银的，一条尾巴，比猫还小，受了伤，跑不远。逮着了，装进这个口袋……」他把那只白布口袋攥得更紧了，「就给我娘一锭。」

「一锭什么？」

「银子。」锁儿道，「先给了一锭定钱……我缝在领子里了，没敢给我娘。给了她，她就知道我要进岭了。我跟她说，我去舅家。」他喘了一阵，「开春……她要把我送去给人放牛……管饭，不管家……两锭银子，她就不用送了。」

小满低头一看，锁儿的领口果然鼓着一块，针脚又粗又歪，是孩子自己缝的。

「他给我这个，」锁儿捏着黄纸的那只手动了一动，「一烧，他就在里头喊我……喊我回来。他喊了，我往回走……天就黑了……下大雨……我找不着路……」他的眼珠子往崖顶上转了一转，「你听见没有？他喊我回来。」

小满想起林子里那三声「……回来……」，又干又深，从头顶上不知什么地方飘下来。他爹说是山鹧鸪。他张了张嘴，道：「听见了。」

锁儿便笑了一下，嘴角刚动，又疼得收了回去：「那他……一会儿……来接我。」

小满没有答。他把锁儿那只捏着黄纸的手拿过来，攥在自己手里。那只手又小又凉，指甲缝里全是树皮渣子，手心里两道新磨出来的口子。小满认得这种口子，他自己手上也有，是刻记号刻的。

「我刻了记号，」锁儿道，「一个圈，里头一横，他教的。刻得低……高的我够不着……」

「我看见了。」小满道，「刻得不歪。」

锁儿没再说话。雨小了一些，崖顶上的水一滴一滴往下漏，滴在石头上。过了好一会儿，锁儿又开了口，声音轻得要把耳朵贴到他嘴边才听得见：「哥。我娘……在……」

就到这里。
story.en:
He crawled over. When his left wrist took his weight the pain blacked out his sight, so he crawled on his right hand and his two knees. Between two boulders at the foot of the cliff lay a child.

The child was smaller than he was — ten at most, all bones, an unlined jacket soaked through and clinging to him, more patches on it than on Xiaoman's. He lay on his back, a stone with its edge upward under the small of his back, his body folded at the waist into a strange shape, both legs sprawled in the muddy water, not moving at all.

One hand clutched a white cloth sack; the other held half a sheet of yellow paper, one end of it burnt.

Hearing someone come, his eyes turned, found Xiaoman, and his lips moved: "…Have you come to fetch me?"

Xiaoman said, "I'm from Shi'ao Village. I fell too."

The little light in the child's eyes went out.

Xiaoman reached to lift him; the moment his hand touched the child's shoulder the child cried "Ah!" — not loud, but it burnt Xiaoman's hand away like fire, and he didn't dare touch him again. His father had said: a creature in the mountains with a broken back can't be moved; move it once and it dies once. So he knelt in the muddy water and leaned forward over the child's face, to keep the rain off it.

"What's your name?"

"Suo'er," the child said. "Suo, like a long-life lock. My ma named me." He took two breaths. "The lock got pawned long ago."

"Which village?"

Suo'er didn't answer that. He said, "…Brother, have you got anything to eat?"

Xiaoman emptied everything out of his jacket. His mother's flatbread, wrapped in cloth, one corner wet; Ahe's egg, still whole. He cracked the egg on a stone, peeled it clean bit by bit, and held the white egg to Suo'er's mouth.

Suo'er opened his mouth but couldn't bite; he only put his nose to it and smelled it, smelled it a long time, and said, "Smells good." And didn't eat. Xiaoman held the egg, not knowing where to put it.

Suo'er suddenly began to talk, one sentence on the heels of the last, fast, as if afraid that if he went slowly there'd be no time for the rest.

"A gentleman in white… came to us… picking children. Picked the thin ones, the ones with no da. He said the stele won't let him in — only lets kids in. He said there's a white fox in the ridge, silver, one tail, smaller than a cat, hurt, can't run far. Catch it, put it in this sack…" He gripped the white cloth sack tighter. "And my ma gets an ingot."

"An ingot of what?"

"Silver," said Suo'er. "He gave one first, on account… I sewed it in my collar. Didn't dare give it to my ma. If I did, she'd know I was going into the ridge. I told her I was going to my uncle's." He panted a while. "Come spring… she's sending me off to mind someone's cows… they feed you, they don't let you home… two ingots, and she wouldn't have to send me."

Xiaoman looked down: sure enough, the child's collar bulged in one place, the stitches big and crooked — a child's own sewing.

"He gave me this," the hand holding the yellow paper stirred. "Burn it, and he calls me from inside it… calls me back. He called, I started back… then it got dark… the rain came… I couldn't find the way…" His eyes rolled up toward the clifftop. "Did you hear? He was calling me back."

Xiaoman remembered those three calls in the forest — "…Come back…" — dry and deep, drifting down from somewhere overhead. His father had said it was a partridge. He opened his mouth and said: "I heard."

Suo'er smiled — the corners of his mouth had barely moved when the pain pulled them back. "Then he'll… soon… come for me."

Xiaoman didn't answer. He took the hand that held the yellow paper and held it in his own. It was small and cold, bark grit under every nail, two fresh raw cuts across the palm. Xiaoman knew those cuts; he had them himself. They came from cutting marks.

"I cut marks," said Suo'er. "A circle, with one stroke inside. He taught me. Cut them low… couldn't reach high…"

"I saw them," Xiaoman said. "They weren't crooked."

Suo'er said no more. The rain had eased; water from the clifftop dripped down, drop by drop, onto the stones. After a long while Suo'er spoke again, so softly Xiaoman had to put his ear to his lips to hear: "Brother. My ma… is in…"

That was as far as it went.

exits.means: holds the dying boy's hand, covers him with the silver leaves, takes the ingot for his mother, checks his own hurts and goes on alone

story.zh:
那只手在小满手里攥了一下，攥得很紧，像要抓住什么往上爬；然后，松了。

小满跪在那里，没有动。他等着那只手再攥一下。雨落在锁儿脸上，落进他睁着的眼睛里，他也不眨。小满伸手替他把眼皮合上，合了两回才合住。

崖根边上长着几棵他不认得的树，叶子是银的，薄得透光。他一片一片摘下来，盖在锁儿身上，从脚盖起，盖到胸口，盖到脸，盖了厚厚一层。叶子落上去，「叮」地响一声，像一只极小的铃铛。他摘了很久，满树的叶子叮叮地响成一片，他也没停。

盖到最后，他把锁儿的领口拆开了。里头是一锭银子，不大，沉甸甸的，锭底錾着一个记号：一个圈，圈里一横——跟林子里齐腰高的那道记号，一模一样。那只白布口袋和那半张烧焦的黄纸，他没有碰，压在了银叶子底下。银子，他揣进了怀里，贴着吴婆婆那块木牌。

锁儿的娘在哪里，他不知道。他只知道这锭银子，是她的。

他在锁儿旁边坐了下来，坐了很久，才想起来自己也是摔下来的。他爹说过，摔了先别急着爬起来，一样一样地查。他先动动手指，手指能动；再动动脚趾，脚趾也能动；膝盖破了，手掌磨掉了一层皮，后背火辣辣的，左手腕肿得老高，断没断，他摸不出来，好在还能动。他这才抬头往上看，崖壁高得望不到顶，一直隐进了雨雾里。

他没有喊，只在心里算：爹被自己拽进了山壁里，没掉下来；他膝盖不好，这么大的雨，他下不来，也不该下来；他会等雨停了，顺着记号回村叫人。四十一道记号，是自己刻的。所以要做的，便是活到那个时候。

十二岁，一个人，在一个从没来过的山谷里，身边躺着一个死了的孩子，天又快黑了。他爹说过，打猎的人在山里迷了路，头一件事是找个地方躲雨，第二件事是生火，第三件事才是害怕。他站起来，去办头一件。

雨小了些。他从地下摸起一片尖石头，扶着崖壁往前走，每走一段，便在崖壁上划一道，好记得回来的路。

走出去不到半里，崖根底下的苔藓里，那片尖石头「当」地碰着了一样硬东西。他扒开苔藓，是一把火镰，锈得通红，鞘子早烂没了，旁边一块火石拿油布裹着，油布也烂了一半。

火镰的木把上拿刀刻着一个字，刻得歪歪扭扭，他认得，是他娘教他写的头一个字：**沈**。他蹲在那里，看了很久。石坳村姓沈的，只有一户；沈家进了黑松岭没回来的，只有一个。

他想起吴婆婆那句「你爷爷走的那年，也从我这门口过」，手心一阵发凉，没敢往下想，把火镰和火石揣进了怀里。这件事，他跟谁也没说。

这山谷很是古怪。地上的草，每一步踩下去，草叶都微微发亮，一圈淡淡的光从他脚底下漾开，又慢慢暗了下去，如同在一面水上走路。他走得很轻很轻，也不知为什么，总觉得这里的东西都在睡觉，不该吵醒了它们。

便在这时，他看见了光。山谷最深处，一片给雨水砸出来的浅坑里，有一点银光一明一暗，一明一暗，像有什么东西在很慢很慢地呼吸。
story.en:
The hand in Xiaoman's squeezed once, hard, as if to catch hold of something and climb; then it let go.

Xiaoman knelt there and didn't move. He waited for the hand to squeeze again. Rain fell on Suo'er's face, into his open eyes, and he didn't blink. Xiaoman reached out and closed his eyelids; it took two tries.

At the foot of the cliff grew a few trees he didn't know, their leaves silver, so thin the light came through. He picked them leaf by leaf and laid them over Suo'er — from the feet up, to the chest, to the face — a thick layer. Each leaf as it landed went *ding*, like a very small bell. He picked for a long time; the whole tree rang with them, and he didn't stop.

Last of all he unpicked Suo'er's collar. Inside was an ingot of silver, small and heavy, a mark chiselled on its base: a circle, with one stroke across it — the very same as the waist-high mark in the forest. The white cloth sack and the half-burnt yellow paper he didn't touch; he left them under the silver leaves. The silver he put inside his jacket, against Granny Wu's token.

Where Suo'er's mother was, he didn't know. He only knew the silver was hers.

He sat down beside Suo'er and sat a long time before he remembered that he had fallen too. His father had said: after a fall, don't rush to get up; check yourself, one thing at a time. First he moved his fingers: they moved. Then his toes: they moved too. His knees were broken open, the skin of his palms scraped off, his back on fire, his left wrist swollen high — broken or not, he couldn't tell, but at least it still moved. Only then did he look up: the cliff rose so high he couldn't see the top; it vanished into the rain and mist.

He didn't shout. He reckoned instead: he'd hauled his father into the rock face — his father hadn't fallen. His father's knee was bad; in rain like this he couldn't come down, and shouldn't; he'd wait for the rain to stop and follow the marks back to the village for help. Forty-one marks, cut by his own hand. So the thing to do was stay alive till then.

Twelve years old, alone, in a valley he'd never seen, a dead child lying beside him, and night about to fall. His father had said: a hunter lost in the mountains first finds shelter from the rain, second makes a fire, and only third gets frightened. He stood up and went to see to the first.

The rain eased a little. He picked a sharp shard of stone up off the ground and went on along the cliff face, and every so far he scratched a line on the rock, so he'd remember the way back.

Less than half a li on, in the moss at the foot of the cliff, the stone shard struck something hard with a *clink*. He scraped the moss away: a fire-steel, rusted bright red, its sheath long rotted away, and beside it a flint wrapped in oilcloth, the oilcloth half rotted too.

On the wooden handle of the fire-steel someone had cut a character with a knife, crooked and uneven, and he knew it — the first character his mother had taught him to write: **Shen**. He crouched there and looked at it a long time. Shi'ao Village had only one household named Shen; and of the Shens who had gone into Black Pine Ridge and not come back, there was only one.

He remembered Granny Wu saying, "The year your grandpa went, he passed my door too," and his palms went cold; he didn't dare think further. He tucked the fire-steel and the flint inside his jacket. He told no one about it.

It was a strange valley. Each step on the grass, the blades glowed faintly, a ring of pale light spreading out from under his foot and slowly dimming, as though he were walking on water. He walked very, very lightly; he couldn't have said why, but he felt everything here was asleep and oughtn't to be woken.

Then he saw the light. At the very bottom of the valley, in a shallow hollow the rain had beaten out, a point of silver light went bright, then dim, bright, then dim — as if something were breathing, very, very slowly.
